[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

This guidance describes how teams using **GitHub Copilot Code Review** as their PR reviewer — alongside either **GitHub Copilot** or **Claude Code** as their AI authoring assistant — should configure AI constructs on both sides of that toolchain and adopt the pre-push convergence practice that prevents multi-round review loops.

GitHub Copilot Code Review and AI coding assistants hold structurally opposing optimization objectives on the same artifact: the author-AI optimizes for delivering change; the reviewer-AI optimizes for finding problems with that change. Without deliberate construct configuration on both sides and a pre-push discipline on the author side, the interaction produces a **convergence loop** — a push-review-fix-push cycle that compounds cost across every PR.

The author side of this practice is an **Agent that orchestrates Skills** — not a single Skill invoked ad hoc. A Skill alone cannot guarantee that planning, independent quality-checking, and convergence run as a mandatory sequence rather than an optional, easily-skipped step; only an Agent's own Execution Instructions can make that sequence non-negotiable. See [Why a Skill Alone Is Insufficient](#why-a-skill-alone-is-insufficient).

This guidance covers:
- How GitHub Copilot Code Review works and what drives its behavior
- The enterprise AI construct taxonomy and where each construct lives
- What constructs teams must author on the **reviewer side** and on the **author side** (for both Copilot and Claude Code users)
- The content requirements for each construct
- The convergence workflow the author-side constructs operationalize
- Named anti-patterns the practice prevents

For strategic context, cost model, and taxonomy of reviewer architectures, see the companion white paper: [Competing Directives: Engineering Convergence in AI-Assisted Review Pipelines](../../../white-papers/engineering/ai-review-pipeline-convergence-strategy.md).

[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#business-context]

### Business Context

The tension between implementation velocity and quality enforcement is not new. Development and QA have always held structurally opposing objectives, managed through sprint-paced process and human negotiation at release boundaries. Traditional peer code review was a separate, team-internal practice moderated by shared colleague context — reviewers understood authorial intent, could negotiate tradeoffs, and focused on maintainability.

AI-assisted review displaces both dynamics simultaneously. Quality enforcement moves from release gates to the commit boundary, applied on every push. The social moderation that made peer review collaborative is absent — Copilot Code Review has no shared history with the author-AI, no understanding of agreed-upon tradeoffs, and no capacity for the negotiation that resolved human QA/Dev tension. The competing directives that teams previously managed through process and relationship are now embedded in the toolchain, triggered at the speed of version control.
page_texts.11:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#technical-context]

### Technical Context

The convergence loop has two structural causes:

1. **Competing optimization objectives** — the author-AI optimizes for delivering change; the reviewer-AI optimizes for finding problems with that change. These objectives are structurally opposed on the same artifact.
2. **Partial-surface fixes** — developers responding to reviewer findings address one finding per push. The reviewer re-evaluates the full diff on the next push and re-raises everything it sees.

The loop is not caused by quality gaps in either tool. Addressing the loop requires deliberate construct configuration on both sides and a pre-push discipline on the author side.

## How GitHub Copilot Code Review Works

Understanding the reviewer's behavior is prerequisite to configuring it correctly and simulating it on the author side.
page_texts.13:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#review-trigger-and-scope]

### Review Trigger and Scope

Copilot Code Review activates as a PR reviewer — manually requested or auto-assigned. When triggered, it evaluates the **full PR diff**: all changed files, all changed lines, across all commits pushed to the branch since the PR was opened. It does not evaluate only the commits since the last review.
page_texts.14:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#stateless-batch-evaluation]

### Stateless Batch Evaluation

Copilot Code Review operates as a **stateless batch reviewer**. On every push:

- It re-reads the complete diff from scratch
- It has no memory of prior review rounds, prior findings, or what was addressed in earlier pushes
- It has no knowledge of what the author intended to fix vs. defer
- Findings deprioritized in a prior round may be escalated in the current round if the diff has changed around them
- New lines introduced by a fix become new surface for evaluation

This is the direct mechanical cause of the convergence loop: each push is a fresh evaluation of an increasingly complex surface.
page_texts.15:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#what-copilot-code-review-reads]

### What Copilot Code Review Reads

Copilot Code Review on GitHub.com reads the following sources from the PR's **head branch** — not the base branch. This means instruction and skill file changes can be tested in the same PR before merging.

| Source | Location | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Repository-wide instructions** | `.github/copilot-instructions.md` | Applied to every review in the repository |
| **Path-specific instructions** | `.github/instructions/**/*.instructions.md` | Applied when the reviewed files match the `applyTo` glob in the instruction file's frontmatter |
| **Agent instructions** | `AGENTS.md` (repository root) | On GitHub.com, Copilot Code Review reads `AGENTS.md` only — it does **not** read `CLAUDE.md` or `GEMINI.md` during PR review (those are read by Copilot cloud agents, not the review bot) |
| **Agent Skills** | `.github/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | Domain expertise loaded by the reviewer |
| **Organization instructions** | Configured in organization Copilot settings | Applied across all repositories in the organization |
| **PR diff** | PR commits | Changed files and lines — the primary evaluation surface |

> **Settings toggle note**: The GitHub repository setting at Settings → Copilot → Code Review is an **on/off toggle** — it controls whether the file-based instructions (above) are applied during review. It is not a separate free-text directive source.

The reviewer reads **nothing** under `.claude/` — that directory is the Claude Code construct namespace and is invisible to Copilot Code Review.

> **Important distinction — `.github/agents/*.agent.md` files**: Agent definition files (`.github/agents/`) define Copilot Chat personas invoked via `@agent-name` in Copilot Chat. They are **not** consumed by the automated PR review bot. A manually-invoked `@ea-reviewer` agent in Copilot Chat uses an agent file; the automated PR review bot that runs on every push uses the sources in the table above.

### Construct Locations

| Construct | Claude Code location | Copilot location | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Skill** | `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | `.github/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | [STD-TEC-AI-001](../../../../standards/technology/ai-development/STD-TEC-AI-001-skill-authoring.md) |

| **Instruction file** | `CLAUDE.md` (root) | `.github/copilot-instructions.md` | [STD-TEC-AI-003](../../../../standards/technology/ai-development/STD-TEC-AI-003-instruction-file.md) |
| **Workflow (Command)** | `.claude/commands/<name>.md` | `.github/prompts/<name>.prompt.md` | [STD-TEC-AI-004](../../../../standards/technology/ai-development/STD-TEC-AI-004-workflow-authoring.md) |
| **Rule** | `.claude/rules/<concern>.md` | `.github/instructions/<concern>.instructions.md` | [STD-TEC-AI-005](../../../../standards/technology/ai-development/STD-TEC-AI-005-file-pattern-instruction.md) |

[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#the-canonical-skill-and-cross-tool-synchronization-pattern]

### The Canonical Skill and Cross-Tool Synchronization Pattern

Skills are canonical in `.claude/skills/` (STD-TEC-AI-001 MR-1). This is the single authoring location regardless of which tool will consume the skill. GitHub Copilot discovers skills at `.github/skills/`, so a **pointer file** at `.github/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` enables Copilot to find the skill at its native path while the full content remains in the canonical Claude Code location.

The pointer file pattern (from [PTN-TEC-AI-003](../../../../patterns/technology/ai-development/PTN-TEC-AI-003-cross-tool-construct-synchronization-pattern.md)):

```
.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md       ← Full skill definition (canonical)
        ↑ (referenced by)
.github/skills/<name>/SKILL.md       ← Pointer file (Copilot discovery)
```

The pointer file is a minimal `SKILL.md` containing frontmatter and a single instruction to read the canonical file:

```markdown
---
name: <skill-name>
description: <same description as canonical, ≤ 300 chars>
---

<One-line operating instruction.>

This skill mirrors the canonical Claude Code skill. Read `.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`
for the full workflow, conventions, and enterprise standards, and apply its guidance to
the current task.

> Single source of truth: `.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`.
```
page_texts.19:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#the-instruction-file-role]

### The Instruction File Role

`.github/copilot-instructions.md` (and `CLAUDE.md`) are **intent-routing context files** — they give the agent repository-wide context and a routing table that maps user intent to the correct Skill or Workflow. They are NOT where Skill content or workflow steps are defined. Behavioral definitions belong in Skill files; operational steps belong in Workflow files.

The instruction file's routing table is what enables auto-invocation: when Copilot (or Claude Code reading `CLAUDE.md`) sees a user intent that matches a trigger phrase, it loads the corresponding Skill or Workflow file.
page_texts.20:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#the-agent-construct-has-no-mandated-cross-tool-parity]

### The Agent Construct Has No Mandated Cross-Tool Parity

Every other construct in the table above — Skill, Instruction file, Workflow, Rule — has a cross-tool synchronization mechanism: [PTN-TEC-AI-003](../../../../patterns/technology/ai-development/PTN-TEC-AI-003-cross-tool-construct-synchronization-pattern.md) designates a source of truth and a derived artifact for each, with parity verified through CI drift checks. **Agent is not one of those four synchronization tiers.** Its absence from PTN-TEC-AI-003's solution table is a deliberate scope boundary of the pattern, not an omission of this guidance.

STD-TEC-AI-002 lists "cross-vendor agent definition parity" in its own Scope, and MR-1.3 documents what a Claude Code equivalent looks like (Skills + `CLAUDE.md` composition, or — for dispatchable sub-agents — a `.claude/agents/*.md` file using the Claude sub-agent frontmatter schema: `name`, `description`, `tools` as a comma-separated string, `disallowedTools`). But the standard contains no MR that requires a `.github/agents/*.agent.md` file to have, or maintain, a `.claude/agents/*.md` counterpart — unlike STD-TEC-AI-001 MR-8, STD-TEC-AI-003 MR-4, STD-TEC-AI-004's Cross-Vendor Parity Model, and STD-TEC-AI-005 MR-7, which each mandate parity for their construct.

**Practical consequence for this guidance**: the Reviewer Agent and the Author Agent described below are both defined as `.github/agents/*.agent.md` files. Claude Code does not read `.github/agents/`, and no standard or automated check requires a `.claude/agents/*.md` counterpart to exist. Teams adopting this guidance must choose deliberately between two options rather than assume parity is already covered:

1. **Skill + `CLAUDE.md` composition (the default)** — Claude Code users invoke the same domain-planning Skill, quality-checking reviewer Skill, and convergence Skill directly, through `CLAUDE.md` routing or an explicit Workflow, without a dispatchable sub-agent file. This delivers the same underlying capability but not the single `@agent-name`-invocation convenience Copilot Chat users get.
2. **A genuine `.claude/agents/<name>.md` counterpart** — a separate file authored in the Claude sub-agent frontmatter schema, not a copy of the Copilot `.agent.md` file (the two schemas are not interchangeable: array `tools` + `agents`/`target`/`handoffs` vs. comma-separated string `tools` + `disallowedTools`). This is optional work a team elects to do; omitting it is not a standards violation, and authoring one does not make it self-synchronizing — it must be maintained by hand against its Copilot counterpart.

Repositories that author a Copilot Author/Reviewer Agent pair and want Claude Code users to have the same one-line invocation experience should track option 2 as a deliberate, separately-scoped follow-up — not an assumed byproduct of authoring the Copilot Agent.

This distinction (constructs #3 and #4 below) is separate from the automated PR-review bot (construct #1), which has no cross-tool consideration at all — it is a GitHub platform feature, not an authored construct pair. See [Four Related, Distinct Constructs](#four-related-distinct-constructs) for how all four fit together.

[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#constructs-required-on-both-sides]

## Constructs Required on Both Sides

Preventing the convergence loop requires constructs on **both** the reviewer side and the author side. Configuring only one side still produces the loop.

| Side | Without constructs | With constructs |
|---|---|---|
| **Reviewer** | Copilot Code Review has no repo-specific quality criteria. It flags issues based on general training that may not reflect the team's agreed standards. Finding behavior is unpredictable — author-side simulation is not possible. | The reviewer Skill (canonical at `.claude/skills/`, discovered by Copilot Code Review through a required pointer file at `.github/skills/`), `AGENTS.md`, path-specific instructions (`.github/instructions/`), and workspace instructions (`.github/copilot-instructions.md`) collectively define what the reviewer looks for and how it ranks findings. Its behavior becomes predictable — a prerequisite for author-side simulation. |
| **Author** | No construct sequences planning, independent quality-checking, and a pre-push consistency pass as a mandatory procedure. Whatever Skill exists runs only when the author-AI happens to recognize a trigger phrase, and even then it re-applies its own criteria to its own output — the same cognitive posture checking itself. The author-AI optimizes for change delivery only. | An **Author Agent** orchestrates, as a mandatory sequence before any commit or push: a domain-planning Skill (decides what to produce and supplies per-type authoring judgment while producing it), a quality-checking subagent backed by a reviewer Skill (independently re-verifies the result against objective criteria — a different cognitive posture than the drafting pass), and the convergence Skill (a final pass for cross-file consistency across everything produced together). See [The Author Agent Pattern](#the-author-agent-pattern). |

---

[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#four-related-distinct-constructs]

### Four Related, Distinct Constructs

"Reviewer" refers to four separate constructs in this guidance, easy to conflate because they share that word. Each has a different file (or no file at all), a different trigger, and a different consumer:

| # | Construct | File / Mechanism | Trigger | Vendor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **GitHub Copilot Code Review** — the automated PR reviewer | GitHub platform feature; not an authored construct | Manually requested or auto-assigned to activate on a PR; re-evaluates automatically on every subsequent push | Copilot-only; no cross-tool counterpart applies |
| 2 | **Reviewer Skill** | `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (canonical) + `.github/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (pointer) | Read by construct #1; also directly usable by Claude Code, by construct #3, and by construct #4 | Both — cross-tool synchronized per PTN-TEC-AI-003 |
| 3 | **Chat-driven Reviewer Agent** | `.github/agents/<name>.agent.md` | Human `@agent-name` invocation in Copilot Chat, OR non-interactive invocation as a subagent an Author Agent declares (STD-TEC-AI-002 MR-10) | Copilot-only — see [The Agent Construct Has No Mandated Cross-Tool Parity](#the-agent-construct-has-no-mandated-cross-tool-parity) |
| 4 | **Claude Code sub-agent** (optional, unmandated) | `.claude/agents/<name>.md` (STD-TEC-AI-002 MR-1.3 schema) | Same two invocation contexts as construct #3, for Claude Code users, only if a team chooses to author it | Claude-only; no parity requirement with construct #3 |

Construct #1 never reads construct #3 or #4 — it reads only construct #2, plus `AGENTS.md` and instruction files. Constructs #3 and #4 both read construct #2 to obtain domain expertise; neither replaces it. The "quality-checking subagent" role in [The Author Agent Pattern](#the-author-agent-pattern) is not a fifth file — it is one of the two invocation contexts of construct #3 (or, if a team has authored one, construct #4).
page_texts.24:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#what-to-author]

### What to Author

Teams configure Copilot Code Review's behavior through the sources it reads from the head branch. The constructs to author are:

1. **A reviewer Skill** — canonical definition at `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, discovered by Copilot Code Review through a required pointer file at `.github/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (see the Reviewer Skill subsection below — both files are mandatory; without the pointer, Copilot Code Review cannot discover the Skill at all) — defines the domain expertise the reviewer applies: quality criteria, finding categories, severity ranking, what constitutes a blocking vs. advisory finding
2. **`AGENTS.md`** (repository root) — provides agent-level context Copilot Code Review reads; this is the only agent-context file the PR review bot reads on GitHub.com (not `CLAUDE.md`)
3. **Path-specific instruction files** (`.github/instructions/**/*.instructions.md`) — scoped reviewer behaviors for specific file patterns; e.g., a file that applies extra security checks only when `.github/workflows/` files are changed
4. **Workspace instructions** (`.github/copilot-instructions.md`) — repository-wide context including the routing table that registers the reviewer Skill for auto-invocation

A **reviewer Agent** (`.github/agents/*.agent.md`) is an optional fifth construct for teams that also want an explicitly invocable `@agent-name` in Copilot Chat — but this does not affect the automated PR review bot's behavior.
page_texts.25:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#reviewer-skill-skillmd]

### Reviewer Skill (`SKILL.md`)

**Canonical location**: `.claude/skills/<reviewer-skill-name>/SKILL.md`
**Copilot pointer**: `.github/skills/<reviewer-skill-name>/SKILL.md`
**Authoring standard**: [STD-TEC-AI-001](../../../../standards/technology/ai-development/STD-TEC-AI-001-skill-authoring.md)

The reviewer Skill encodes the criteria Copilot Code Review applies to evaluate changed artifacts. It must define:

**Required content (per STD-TEC-AI-001):**

1. **YAML frontmatter** — `name` and `description` fields; `description` is the invocation trigger used for auto-invocation; ≤ 300 characters
2. **Operating instruction** — single imperative sentence immediately after frontmatter (e.g., "Review changed artifacts for quality, standards conformance, and internal consistency")
3. **Scope** — `$ARGUMENTS` routing (PR number, branch, working tree), explicit positive and negative scope boundaries
4. **Workflow** — analysis phases the reviewer follows: how to identify changed artifacts, what quality dimensions to check, how to rank and present findings
5. **Guidelines** — behavioral constraints: what the reviewer owns vs. reads, delegation directives for out-of-scope work, at least three behavioral constraints

**Domain content the reviewer Skill should define:**
page_texts.26:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#risk-based-fitness-for-purpose-review-behavior]

### Risk-Based, Fitness-for-Purpose Review Behavior

Reviewer-side constructs should enforce a risk-based review posture that optimizes for measurable quality outcomes instead of stylistic perfectionism.

- Evaluate changes for fitness for purpose: correctness, security, architecture alignment, performance, and reliability in the repository context.
- Flag only concrete defects, objective inconsistencies, or explicit hard-requirement violations.
- Do not raise findings for naming preference, subjective elegance rewrites, or micro-optimizations when the implementation is safe, readable, and functionally correct.
- When multiple valid implementation approaches satisfy repository constraints, preserve architect/implementer autonomy; require change only when a concrete risk is present.

This risk-based philosophy must be represented explicitly in workspace instructions (`.github/copilot-instructions.md`) so the automated reviewer and the author-side convergence practice operate against the same quality bar.

- **Quality dimensions** to evaluate (e.g., internal consistency, cross-file coherence, authoring constraint compliance, standards conformance, normative-authority correctness)
- **Finding severity model** — what distinguishes a blocking finding (must be resolved before merge) from an advisory finding (recommendation, not a gate)
- **Scope boundary** — what artifact types and file patterns the reviewer evaluates, and what it explicitly does not evaluate (e.g., generated files, vendored code, files excluded by the team)
- **Finding format** — how the reviewer presents its output so authors receive actionable, unambiguous findings

**Example frontmatter:**

```yaml
---
name: reviewer
description: Use when reviewing a PR, diff, or staged changes containing architecture artifacts or code. Checks authoring compliance, internal consistency, and cross-document coherence. Ranks findings and gives Approve/Request Changes verdict.
---
```
page_texts.27:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#reviewer-skill--copilot-pointer]

### Reviewer Skill — Copilot Pointer

**Location**: `.github/skills/<reviewer-skill-name>/SKILL.md`
**Purpose**: Enables Copilot Code Review to discover the reviewer Skill at its native `.github/skills/` path — without this file, the automated PR review bot cannot read the reviewer Skill at all, regardless of how complete the canonical file is

This is a lightweight pointer file following the cross-tool synchronization pattern ([PTN-TEC-AI-003](../../../../patterns/technology/ai-development/PTN-TEC-AI-003-cross-tool-construct-synchronization-pattern.md)) — the same pattern the convergence Skill pointer follows:

```markdown
---
name: <reviewer-skill-name>
description: <same description as canonical, ≤ 300 chars>
---

Review changed artifacts for quality, standards conformance, and internal consistency.

This skill mirrors the canonical Claude Code skill. Read `.claude/skills/<reviewer-skill-name>/SKILL.md`
for the full workflow, conventions, and enterprise standards, and apply its guidance to
the current task.

> Single source of truth: `.claude/skills/<reviewer-skill-name>/SKILL.md`.
```

The description must match the canonical Skill's frontmatter exactly so Copilot Code Review and Claude Code apply the same quality criteria.

[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#reviewer-agent--chat-driven-and-subagent-use-copilot-only-construct]

### Reviewer Agent — Chat-Driven and Subagent Use (Copilot-Only Construct)

**Location**: `.github/agents/<reviewer-agent-name>.agent.md`
**Authoring standard**: [STD-TEC-AI-002](../../../../standards/technology/ai-development/STD-TEC-AI-002-agent-definition.md)

> **Important**: Agent definition files (`.github/agents/*.agent.md`) are **not** consumed by the automated PR review bot (construct #1). They are a separate, Copilot-only construct (construct #3 — see [Four Related, Distinct Constructs](#four-related-distinct-constructs)). Authoring a reviewer Agent does not change how the automated review bot behaves — that behavior is governed entirely by the reviewer Skill, instruction files, and `AGENTS.md` described above.

This Agent has exactly two invocation contexts, and both are **file-path-scoped, not PR-number-scoped**:

1. **Human-invoked, chat-driven use** — a developer types e.g. `@ea-reviewer Check decisions/application/ADR-APP-042-event-streaming.md` in Copilot Chat for an ad hoc quality check on a draft or specific file(s), independent of any PR — useful before a PR even exists.
2. **Agent-invoked, subagent use** — an Author Agent declares this same Agent as a subagent (`agents:` frontmatter field per STD-TEC-AI-002 MR-10) and invokes it non-interactively as the independent quality-check step in [The Author Agent Pattern](#the-author-agent-pattern), before anything is committed or pushed.

In both contexts the Agent: loads the reviewer Skill to obtain domain expertise, evaluates the specified file(s) against that Skill's quality criteria, ranks findings, and presents a verdict.

**This Agent must never reimplement PR-number-bound review** — fetching a PR by number, or classifying "initial review" vs. "re-review" vs. "respond to reviewer clarification." That workflow belongs entirely to construct #1, GitHub Copilot Code Review. An Agent that reimplements it duplicates the automated reviewer, reintroduces the same stateless-batch-evaluation behavior this guidance's convergence practice exists to get ahead of, and forfeits the file-path-only scope both invocation contexts above require. A reviewer Agent whose only entry points require a PR number cannot serve either context in this section.

The agent file must define:

- **YAML frontmatter**: `description` (≤ 500 characters), `tools` array (read, search, execute), and optionally `model`
- **Persona and principles**: how the reviewer behaves — standards-enforcing, evidence-based, scope-disciplined, actionable
- **Intent classification** *(only if the Agent supports more than one distinct task type)*: how to distinguish file-path-scoped review task types from user input (e.g., single-file check vs. multi-file check vs. re-check after revision) — never a PR-number task type
- **Routing table** *(only if the Agent supports more than one distinct task type)*: which workflow file to load for each file-path-scoped task type
- **Skill loading instruction**: explicit step to load the reviewer Skill before any evaluation (e.g., "Load the reviewer Skill: Read `.github/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`")
- **Execution instructions**: numbered steps covering skill loading, task classification/routing (if applicable), and execution

**Fixed-workflow exception**: A reviewer Agent scoped to a single task — quality-check the artifact(s) identified in `$ARGUMENTS` or an invoking Agent's plan, with no other task shape — is exempt from Intent classification and the Routing table per the STD-TEC-AI-006 fixed-workflow exception (see `ea-reviewer.agent.md` and `ai-review.agent.md`); its Execution instructions describe the single fixed flow directly.

[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#why-author-side-constructs-are-separate-from-reviewer-side-constructs]

### Why Author-Side Constructs Are Separate from Reviewer-Side Constructs

Author-side constructs run before pushing. They prompt the author-AI to simulate the reviewer's perspective — to find and resolve the issues the reviewer will find before the push triggers the review cycle. This is a fundamentally different concern from reviewer-side constructs, which run after pushing.

Neither side's constructs affect the other's behavior. The reviewer reads nothing under `.claude/`. Claude Code reads nothing under `.github/skills/reviewer/`. The two construct sets work in parallel on opposite sides of the push boundary.
page_texts.32:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#why-a-skill-alone-is-insufficient]

### Why a Skill Alone Is Insufficient

Earlier revisions of this guidance treated a single convergence Skill, invoked ad hoc by the author-AI when it recognized a trigger phrase, as the complete author-side answer. In practice this under-delivers for three structural reasons:

1. **A Skill has no orchestration authority.** A Skill executes one cognitive operation and returns a result — it cannot itself decide to invoke a second Skill for an independent check, or guarantee that a planning pass happens before a drafting pass. Sequencing multiple cognitive operations into a mandatory procedure is what an Agent does; a Skill cannot do this for itself.
2. **Self-invocation is not independent verification.** A Skill re-applying its own criteria to its own output is the same cognitive posture checking itself — it does not catch the class of error a genuinely separate check catches (bias toward the author's own framing, blind spots in the author's own reasoning). Effective quality assurance requires a second, differently-postured pass, not a repetition of the first.
3. **Ad hoc invocation is easily skipped.** A Skill only runs when the author-AI recognizes a trigger phrase in the instruction file's routing table. Under time pressure, or when the author-AI is confident it doesn't need the check, the invocation is easy to omit. A step embedded in an Agent's Execution Instructions is a mandatory part of the Agent's own procedure — it cannot be silently skipped the way an optionally-triggered Skill can.

The fix is not a better Skill. It is an **Agent that orchestrates Skills as a mandatory sequence**, with an independent quality-check step that a different cognitive posture — not the same drafting pass — performs before anything is committed.
page_texts.33:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#the-author-agent-pattern]

### The Author Agent Pattern

The author side of the convergence practice is an Agent — not a Skill — that orchestrates three things, in this order, every time it produces or revises an artifact:

1. **A domain-planning Skill** — decides *what* needs to be produced (which artifact, module, component, or change) and supplies the per-type authoring judgment applied while producing it. This Skill encodes genuine domain expertise, and that expertise is specific to what the Agent produces — it is not a generic template. A documentation-authoring Agent's planning Skill decides which governance artifact type answers a stated need and what makes an instance of that type sound. A code-authoring Agent's planning Skill decides which service or module boundary a change belongs in and what makes an implementation of that boundary sound — test coverage, error handling, interface contract discipline. The construct shape is identical; the domain content is not, and should not be copied across domains.
2. **A quality-checking subagent, backed by a reviewer Skill** — after drafting, the Agent invokes a *separate* subagent (STD-TEC-AI-002 MR-10 Subagent Composition) whose sole job is to independently verify the drafted or revised content against objective criteria: structural/template conformance, traceable claims, and — for a revision — that every change stays within the scope of what was actually requested. This subagent applies the same reviewer Skill that also backs the reviewer side of this practice (see [Reviewer-Side Constructs](#reviewer-side-constructs)), so the pre-push check and the post-push GitHub Copilot Code Review apply the same quality bar. This subagent must have **no dependency on a PR existing** — it operates on drafted content directly, before anything is written, committed, or pushed. A construct whose only entry points require an existing PR number cannot serve this role (see the note in [Reviewer Agent — Chat-Driven and Subagent Use](#reviewer-agent--chat-driven-and-subagent-use-copilot-only-construct)).
3. **The convergence Skill** — once planning and the quality check are complete, the Agent runs the convergence workflow (Phases 0–4, below) once across every file touched in the current change, catching cross-file propagation gaps between everything produced together — not just consistency within a single file.

Only after all three steps complete does the Agent present its output for confirmation and, once confirmed, allow the commit/push to proceed. GitHub Copilot Code Review then performs its own independent evaluation on the pushed PR — this remains the final validation layer, not the primary quality mechanism. The Agent's job is to make that final review a formality by resolving what the reviewer-AI would have found, before it ever sees the diff.

This Agent construct itself has no mandated Claude Code counterpart — see [The Agent Construct Has No Mandated Cross-Tool Parity](#the-agent-construct-has-no-mandated-cross-tool-parity). Claude Code users get the same three-step sequence only if the team invokes the underlying Skills directly (the default) or separately authors and maintains a `.claude/agents/*.md` sub-agent — neither is automatic.
page_texts.34:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#the-pattern-is-domain-agnostic]

### The Pattern Is Domain-Agnostic

This Agent-orchestrates-Skills shape is the same regardless of what the Agent produces. A documentation-authoring Agent (governance artifacts, architecture records, standards) and a code-authoring Agent (services, modules, features) both need: a planning Skill scoped to their own domain's taxonomy and quality bar, a quality-checking subagent backed by a reviewer Skill scoped to their own domain's objective criteria, and the shared convergence Skill for cross-file consistency. Engineering teams building a code-authoring Agent should not copy a documentation-oriented planning Skill's content — they need their own, scoped to their language, service boundaries, and test/coverage conventions — but the orchestration shape (Agent → plan → draft → independent quality check → converge → confirm) is identical.
page_texts.35:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#convergence-skill--claude-code]

### Convergence Skill — Claude Code

**Canonical location**: `.claude/skills/<convergence-skill-name>/SKILL.md`
**Authoring standard**: [STD-TEC-AI-001](../../../../standards/technology/ai-development/STD-TEC-AI-001-skill-authoring.md)
**Purpose**: Instructs Claude Code to perform the convergence workflow — an open-comment triage pre-step when reviewing an active PR, followed by the four core phases — before staging or committing any change (see [The Convergence Workflow](#the-convergence-workflow) for the full phase breakdown)

This is the full-implementation Skill. The Copilot pointer (below) references this file as its authoritative source.

**Required content:**

1. **YAML frontmatter** — description must trigger on: "before staging or committing", "changed concept description", "open PR review comments", "cross-file change"
2. **Scope** — when to run (see Workflow trigger conditions below), what it covers (the open-comment triage pre-step plus the four core phases), what it does not cover (design decisions about what correct content should be — delegate those to `/documenter` or `/architect`; the Skill applies unambiguous fixes itself)
3. **Workflow** — the open-comment triage pre-step and the four core phases (see The Convergence Workflow section)
4. **Anti-patterns** — named failure modes the Skill prevents (see Common Pitfalls section); described with enough specificity that Claude Code recognizes them mid-session and interrupts the pattern
5. **Guidelines** — ownership (reads changed files, applies unambiguous consistency fixes directly), delegation (delegates design decisions about what correct content should be to `/documenter` or `/architect`; delegates commits to the git workflow), at least three behavioral constraints
6. **Skill collaboration table** — showing this Skill gates the commit and push steps

**Capabilities that significantly improve effectiveness — include in the Skill definition:**

- **Morphological variant search** — the Skill should instruct Claude Code to search for inflected forms of any changed concept (e.g. `register` → `registered`, `registering`, `registration`). The reviewer reads the full file and will find every form; searching only the exact phrase used in the edit will miss occurrences that carry the same meaning and will generate review comments.
- **Pre-existing inconsistency scan** — the Skill should instruct Claude Code to check for prose/structure mismatches on concepts not changed, in every file it touches. The reviewer reads the whole file on every push; a pre-existing mismatch in a touched file will be flagged even if the diff did not introduce it. When an author touches a file, they adopt responsibility for its full internal state.
- **False fix detection** — the Skill should instruct Claude Code to verify mechanically-specific reviewer claims (path depth, field count, list length, link resolution) independently before editing. A reviewer comment that makes an incorrect structural claim does not become correct by receiving a fix — editing correct content to satisfy an incorrect claim introduces a defect.

page_texts.39:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#the-convergence-workflow]

## The Convergence Workflow

This is the canonical convergence workflow the convergence Skill operationalizes: a conditional open-comment triage pre-step (Phase 0, active PR review cycles only) followed by four core phases (Phases 1–4) that always apply regardless of whether a PR is open. Teams author this content into their convergence Skill's Workflow section.
page_texts.40:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#when-to-run]

### When to Run

Run before any commit or push whenever:

- A concept's description was changed in a file (value, condition, exception, classification)
- A requirement or conditional was added or removed
- A change to one file logically implies a change to another
- Open PR review comments are being processed — treat all open comments as a single batch, not one at a time
page_texts.41:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#phase-0-triage-open-comments-active-pr-only]

### Phase 0: Triage Open Comments (Active PR Only)

Phase 0 is a conditional pre-step, not one of the four core phases below — it applies only when the workflow is running against an active PR with open review comments. Phases 1–4 always apply.

Before building any occurrence inventory, classify each open review comment:

| Status | Condition | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Live** | The issue is still present in the current file | Include in Phase 1 occurrence inventory |
| **Stale** | The issue no longer exists in the current file | Resolve comment, no edit — do not re-introduce the gap to satisfy a resolved finding |
| **Deferred** | The issue is real but not being fixed in this push | Record explicitly; skip Phase 1 for this comment |
| **False Positive** | The comment makes a mechanically verifiable claim that is independently confirmed incorrect | No edit; record as a false positive using the same path as Stale; skip Phase 1 |

Do not edit correct content to satisfy a stale comment. Do not build an occurrence inventory for a stale comment — doing so leads directly to the False Fix anti-pattern.
page_texts.42:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#phase-1-map-the-change-surface]

### Phase 1: Map the Change Surface

For each changed file:

1. Read the **entire file** — not just the diff lines
2. Run the pre-existing inconsistency scan: for every concept that has both a prose description and a structured representation (diagram node, table cell, step list item), verify they agree — even for concepts not changed in this edit. The reviewer reads the whole file; a pre-existing mismatch will be flagged.
3. State the concept changed: "I changed [what] in [file] to [new value/condition]"
4. Search for all parallel occurrences — including morphological variants of the changed concept:
   - Prose descriptions and overviews
   - Table cells and component lists
   - Diagram nodes and edge labels
   - Numbered step lists and procedures
   - Examples, scenarios, and use cases
   - TL;DR and key-points sections
5. For any structured element where a new entry will be added: read the entire element first to confirm no entry for the same concept already exists — if one does, update or merge rather than adding alongside
6. Build an occurrence inventory:

```text
Concept: [what changed]
File: [filename]

| # | Section     | Type       | Current text (excerpt)   | Status    |
|---|-------------|------------|--------------------------|-----------|
| 1 | Overview    | prose      | "...old statement..."    | ✓ updated |
| 2 | Components  | table cell | "...old value..."        | ❌ pending |
| 3 | Step 4      | list item  | "...old instruction..."  | ❌ pending |
```
page_texts.43:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#phase-2-cross-file-propagation]

### Phase 2: Cross-File Propagation

For each changed concept, find all other **changed files in the PR diff** that enumerate the same concept. Scope is the full PR diff — not just files being edited in the current session. A file touched in push 1 will be re-reviewed in push 10; the reviewer evaluates the full diff on every evaluation.

A propagation is complete only when every file in the diff that enumerates the concept lists the same items as the authoritative source.
page_texts.44:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#phase-2a-removal-propagation-when-the-diff-contains-deletions]

### Phase 2a: Removal Propagation (When the Diff Contains Deletions)

When the diff deletes a Skill directory, Command file, or Prompt file, search the **entire repository** — not just changed files — for orphaned references to the removed construct: slash invocations (`/eap-lint`), canonical file paths (`.claude/commands/eap-lint.md`, `.github/prompts/eap-lint.prompt.md`), and prose references. Use construct-specific search patterns — a search pattern shaped for Skills will not find dangling Command or Prompt references. Exclude coincidental name collisions (a variable or role name that happens to match). Update or deprecate every genuine hit before merging; a deleted construct that is still referenced elsewhere is not fully removed. Skip this sub-phase when the diff contains no deletions.
page_texts.45:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#phase-3-resolve-all-gaps]

### Phase 3: Resolve All Gaps

Fix every ❌ in the occurrence inventories. For each gap deliberately not being fixed:

1. Write a brief note explaining the deferral: what the issue is, why it is not being resolved in this push, where it is tracked
2. Record it — as a PR description note, a comment on the open review comment, or a linked follow-up issue
3. Mark the occurrence as explicitly deferred

Do not commit until all occurrence inventories show ✓ or explicitly recorded deferrals.
page_texts.46:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#phase-4-pre-commit-verification-checklist]

### Phase 4: Pre-Commit Verification Checklist

Before any `git commit`, verify for each changed file:

- [ ] Every diagram matches the text in the same section
- [ ] Every table cell matches the prose description of the same concept in the same file
- [ ] No section uses an old, unqualified version of a concept that was qualified elsewhere in the same file
- [ ] For any structured element where a new entry was added: no duplicate entry exists for the same concept
- [ ] Every heading still accurately describes its section body after conditional qualifications were added
- [ ] Every `MUST`/`SHALL` normative statement is not presented as already binding or enforceable while its own document status (or a cited authority's status) is `draft`/`proposed` — a `draft` artifact is expected to propose Mandatory Requirements; the defect is claiming current enforceability, not the presence of proposed MUST/SHALL wording
- [ ] Every open review comment is either resolved or explicitly deferred with a recorded note

Across all changed files (scope: full PR diff):
- [ ] Every enumeration of a changed concept is consistent across all files that enumerate it
- [ ] No file still uses the old, unconditional version of a concept that was conditionally qualified in another file

page_texts.47:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#common-pitfalls]

## Common Pitfalls

These are the named anti-patterns the convergence Skill must define and prevent. Teams should name them explicitly in the Skill definition so the author-AI recognizes them mid-session and interrupts the pattern.
page_texts.48:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#the-one-comment-per-push-fix]

### The One-Comment-Per-Push Fix

A review comment arrives. The developer fixes that one comment and pushes. The reviewer re-evaluates the full diff, re-raises all remaining findings, and surfaces new issues on recently changed lines. The loop does not close.

**Prevention**: Phase 0 classifies all open comments before any editing begins. All live comments are processed as a single batch. One push after addressing the full live surface — not one push per comment.
page_texts.49:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#the-flagged-line-only-fix]

### The Flagged-Line-Only Fix

The reviewer flags line 97. The developer reads and fixes line 97 only. Lines 42, 118, and 203 describe the same concept and are not checked. The reviewer flags them on the next push.

**Prevention**: A review comment points to a symptom, not a concept. Phase 1 finds all occurrences of the underlying concept in the file — not just the flagged line.
page_texts.50:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#the-additive-fix]

### The Additive Fix

A table or list needs a new entry for a changed concept. Without reading the full element first, a new entry is added alongside an existing entry for the same concept. The element now has duplicate rows. The reviewer flags the duplication.

**Prevention**: Before inserting any new entry into a structured element, read the entire element. If an entry for the same concept exists, update or merge it.
page_texts.51:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#the-silent-deferral]

### The Silent Deferral

A review comment points to a real issue the developer decides not to fix in this push. No note is made. The reviewer re-raises it on every subsequent push because it cannot distinguish "decided not to fix" from "missed."

**Prevention**: Phase 3 requires an explicit deferral record for every gap not being fixed. Record it — resolve the review comment with an explanation, add a PR description note, or link a follow-up issue.
page_texts.52:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#the-false-fix]

### The False Fix

The reviewer makes a mechanical claim — a path is one level too deep, a field count is wrong, a link resolves incorrectly. The developer accepts the claim, edits the file to match, and pushes. The original was correct; the edit introduces a defect.

**Prevention**: For any comment making a structural or mechanical claim, verify independently before editing. Count the items in the authoritative source, trace the path, check a neighboring file that uses the same pattern. A reviewer comment that is factually wrong does not become correct by receiving a fix.
page_texts.53:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#the-accidental-adopter]

### The Accidental Adopter

A developer touches a file to fix one line. The file had a pre-existing prose/diagram mismatch they did not introduce. The reviewer reads the whole file on the next push and flags the pre-existing mismatch. The developer is blamed for a gap they inherited.

**Prevention**: The pre-existing inconsistency scan in Phase 1 catches these before the reviewer does. When you touch a file, you adopt responsibility for its full internal state.

---
page_texts.55:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#use-case-1-single-file-change-active-pr]

### Use Case 1: Single-File Change, Active PR

An architect adds a conditional exception to a requirement. The condition is added to the solution description prose but not to the architecture diagram, the components table, or the interactions step list.

**Without the practice**: The reviewer flags the diagram, table, and step list as contradicting the updated prose. Three additional push-review cycles follow.

**With the practice**: Phase 1 builds an occurrence inventory covering all four representations. All three missing locations are resolved before the first push. The reviewer confirms consistency.
page_texts.56:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#use-case-2-multiple-open-comments-active-pr]

### Use Case 2: Multiple Open Comments, Active PR

A PR has six open review comments across three files. The developer addresses comment 1 and pushes. The reviewer re-raises comments 2–6 plus surfaces new issues on the recently changed lines.

**Without the practice**: The loop extends across six or more push-review cycles.

**With the practice**: Phase 0 classifies all six comments as Live, Stale, or Deferred. All live issues are resolved in one edit session; deferrals are recorded. One push closes the loop.
page_texts.57:
[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#use-case-3-cross-file-concept-change]

### Use Case 3: Cross-File Concept Change

A standard gains a new required field. The authoritative definition is updated, but three patterns in the same PR diff also enumerate that field and are not updated.

**Without the practice**: The reviewer flags all three patterns for omitting the new field.

**With the practice**: Phase 2 maps the field enumeration across all changed files. All three patterns are updated before pushing.

### Construct Authoring Governance

All constructs authored for the convergence practice must conform to the enterprise AI construct authoring standards:

| Construct | Standard | Quality checklist |
|---|---|---|
| Author Agent | STD-TEC-AI-002 | Agent must pass the MR-1 through MR-10 compliance checklist, including MR-10 Subagent Composition for the quality-checking subagent declaration |
| Domain-planning Skill | STD-TEC-AI-001 | Skill must pass the MR-1 through MR-8 compliance checklist; must encode genuine domain judgment (reasoning steps), not reference tables alone |
| Convergence Skill (canonical) | STD-TEC-AI-001 | Skill must pass the MR-1 through MR-8 compliance checklist before use |
| Convergence Skill (Copilot pointer) | STD-TEC-AI-001 | Pointer must have valid frontmatter; `name` and `description` must match canonical |
| Reviewer Skill (canonical) | STD-TEC-AI-001 | Skill must pass the MR-1 through MR-8 compliance checklist before use |
| Reviewer Skill (Copilot pointer) | STD-TEC-AI-001 | Pointer must have valid frontmatter; `name` and `description` must match canonical — required for Copilot Code Review to discover the Skill at all |
| Reviewer Agent / quality-checking subagent | STD-TEC-AI-002 | Agent must pass the MR-1 through MR-7 compliance checklist; if also used as a subagent, its scope must accept file paths directly and must not depend on an existing PR |
| Convergence Command/Prompt (if authored) | STD-TEC-AI-004 | Command and Prompt pair must both exist; cross-vendor parity required |

[strategy/guidance/technology/implementation/GUID-TECH-IMPL-012-ai-review-convergence-practice-guidance.md#risk-management]

### Risk Management

| Risk | Description | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Reviewer Skill divergence | The reviewer Skill is updated on one team's repo but not synchronized to a shared library | Platform team maintains a shared reviewer Skill library; teams reference it rather than authoring independent versions |
| Missing pointer file | Canonical Skill (reviewer or convergence) exists in `.claude/skills/` but no pointer file in `.github/skills/` — Copilot cannot discover the Skill | PTN-TEC-AI-003 cross-tool sync validation; `/eap-ai-sync` detects missing pointer files |
| Incomplete author-side adoption | Some team members use the convergence Skill; others do not | Add convergence Skill invocation to the team Definition of Done for AI-assisted PRs; register in both instruction files for auto-invocation |
| False fix from reviewer claim | A reviewer comment makes an incorrect mechanical claim | The False Fix anti-pattern and Phase 4 checklist provide the verification discipline |
| Assumed Agent parity | A team assumes the Author/Reviewer Agent automatically has a Claude Code counterpart the way Skills, Instructions, Workflows, and Rules do | No such assumption is valid — see [The Agent Construct Has No Mandated Cross-Tool Parity](#the-agent-construct-has-no-mandated-cross-tool-parity); teams must deliberately choose Skill-composition or author a separate `.claude/agents/*.md` file |
